children.innerHTML:
We teach the breath.
The sea teaches the rest.
Two coaches, one shed of ropes and buoys, and a bay that drops to forty-two metres a short swim from the pier. That's the whole school. It's enough.

attributes.alt: Nils Berge, Depth coach, photographed underwater

children.innerHTML: Ten years of competition taught Nils exactly how much of freediving happens from the neck up. He teaches the calm first and the metres second, and has never once shouted through a snorkel.

attributes.alt: Ada Kealoha, Head of breath, photographed underwater

children.innerHTML: Ada starts every course on dry land with coffee and a heart-rate monitor, proving you can halve your pulse before your toes get wet. Students call her sessions naps. She allows it.
Portraits taken where we actually live
Ninety seconds from the pier to the house reef

attributes.alt: The white village above Anchor Bay

children.innerHTML: Anchor Bay, past the fish sheds
North shore, ten minutes on foot from the village square. Water from 19° in spring to 24° in August, forty-two metres to the sand, and visibility that embarrasses swimming pools.
Follow the buoys past the pier. If you reach the chapel you have gone too far, which everyone does exactly once.
Every diver has eyes on them, every metre, every time. The surface is a team sport.
We dive attached, we dive the plan, and the plan is written before the wetsuits go on.
Relaxation makes metres. Ego takes them away, usually with interest.
Every session ends with names, numbers and dinner plans. The logbook comes second.
first dive past the reflex, surfaced laughing
hands-free equalisation, finally, after two years
couldn't put her face in the water on day one
the plate, on his fortieth birthday, easy as breakfast
her whole course underwater smiling, which is against the rules
Every metre in this book was earned slowly, which is the only way metres keep.
